description: Quality rules for mini-apps designed primarily for phones (iOS / Android). Focus on touch ergonomics, viewport sizing, no-keyboard interaction, gesture handling, and thumb-reach UX. Apply when the goal mentions 'mobile', 'phone', 'iOS', 'Android', 'touch', or any classic mobile-game name (PvZ, jetpack side-scroller, match-three puzzle, tap-to-flap arcade, etc).

guidelines.rule: Use the `viewport` meta tag set for mobile fit: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no, viewport-fit=cover">`. The `viewport-fit=cover` extends content under the iOS notch / dynamic island; `user-scalable=no` prevents accidental pinch-zoom during fast gameplay.
guidelines.why: Without this meta tag, mobile browsers default to a 980px desktop viewport scaled down — text microscopic, touch targets unreachable. Without `user-scalable=no`, double-tap on game canvas zooms instead of fires.
examples: <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, maximum-scale=1, user-scalable=no, viewport-fit=cover">

guidelines.rule: Touch targets MUST be at least 44×44 logical pixels (Apple HIG) and ideally 48×48 (Material). Apply this to every button, draggable, and tap-zone — even 'small' icon-only buttons. Add invisible padding (`padding: 12px;` on a 24px icon) to grow the hit area without changing visual size.
guidelines.why: Sub-44px targets are painfully easy to miss with a finger. The visual element can be 16px but the interactive element needs to be 44px+ via padding or absolute-positioned hit zone overlay.
examples: button { min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px; padding: 12px; }
// hit-zone overlay pattern: a transparent <div> behind the icon, sized 44x44, with the same onclick

guidelines.rule: Use `100dvh` (dynamic viewport height), NOT `100vh`, for full-screen layouts. Account for safe-area insets via `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` etc. so controls aren't hidden behind the iOS home indicator or Android nav bar.
guidelines.why: 100vh on iOS Safari includes the URL bar — content gets pushed below the fold or jumps when the bar collapses. dvh is the dynamic value; safe-area-inset prevents fixed-bottom controls from being half-hidden behind the home indicator.
examples: .game-container { height: 100dvh; }
.bottom-controls { padding-bottom: max(12px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom)); }
@supports not (height: 100dvh) { .game-container { height: 100vh; } } /* iOS < 16 fallback */

guidelines.rule: Place primary action controls in the BOTTOM HALF of the screen (within thumb reach when holding a phone one-handed). Headers, scores, and read-only info go up top. Critical buttons (Fire, Tap-to-Jump, Plant, Spin) belong in the bottom 40-50% of the viewport, ideally bottom 25%.
guidelines.why: Top of phone screen is unreachable for a one-handed thumb. The reachable arc is the bottom hemisphere. Mobile games that put controls at the top fail one-handed play.
examples: Top bar (header): score, lives, wave counter — read-only
Center: game canvas / playfield
Bottom 25%: primary action buttons (Fire, Jump, Plant Card)
For PvZ-style: plant cards in a ROW at the bottom, not a sidebar

guidelines.rule: Use `pointerdown` events (not `click`), and call `event.preventDefault()` to suppress the 300ms tap-delay AND the synthetic mouse events. For gesture-heavy games (drag, swipe), use the Pointer Events API uniformly; don't mix touch + mouse handlers.
guidelines.why: click has a 300ms delay on mobile (waiting to see if it's a double-tap). pointerdown is instant. preventDefault stops the synthetic mousedown that fires after touchend, which would otherwise double-trigger handlers.
examples: btn.addEventListener('pointerdown', e => { e.preventDefault(); fire(); }, { passive: false })
Drag pattern: pointerdown sets `dragging = true`; pointermove updates position; pointerup clears.
For canvas: get coords via e.offsetX/Y or rect-relative — touch.clientX requires manual canvas-rect math.

guidelines.rule: Disable iOS text-selection on game canvas + buttons: `user-select: none; -webkit-user-select: none; -webkit-touch-callout: none;`. Disable the iOS tap-highlight rectangle: `-webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent;`. Apply globally on `body` + game elements.
guidelines.why: Long-press on a button shows an iOS text-selection menu OR copy/paste callout — both interrupt gameplay. The grey tap-highlight flashes on every tap, looks unprofessional in a polished game.
examples: * { -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; -webkit-touch-callout: none; -webkit-user-select: none; user-select: none; }
Canvas: also touch-action: none; to suppress browser scroll/zoom gestures during gameplay

guidelines.rule: PORTRAIT orientation by default for mobile mini-apps. Use a media query OR JavaScript orientation check to render an 'rotate phone' message if landscape is required and the user is portrait (or vice versa). Most casual mobile games are PORTRAIT — match user expectation.
guidelines.why: Phones are held in portrait 80%+ of the time. Landscape-only mobile games friction the casual player. PvZ, match-three puzzle, jetpack side-scroller: all portrait. The exception is racing / shooters that need wide screen — those should explicitly prompt for landscape.
examples: @media (orientation: landscape) { .rotate-prompt { display: block; } .game { display: none; } }
Default game container: max-width: 480px; height: 100dvh; (portrait phone aspect)
Layout in CSS grid rows: header / playfield / controls — vertically stacked, never sidebar columns

guidelines.rule: Use `requestAnimationFrame` with delta-time for game loops. ALSO: pause/resume the loop on `visibilitychange` so battery doesn't drain when the user switches tabs. Save game state to localStorage on `pagehide` (more reliable than `beforeunload` on mobile).
guidelines.why: Mobile users tab away constantly (notifications, lock screen). Without visibilitychange handling, the game runs in the background draining battery. pagehide is the only event that fires reliably when iOS Safari kills a tab — beforeunload is unreliable.
examples: document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', () => { if (document.hidden) pauseGame(); else resumeGame(); })
window.addEventListener('pagehide', () => localStorage.setItem('gameState', JSON.stringify(state)));
// Resume from saved state on load: const saved = localStorage.getItem('gameState'); if (saved) state = JSON.parse(saved);

guidelines.rule: Haptic feedback on critical taps via `navigator.vibrate(20)` (Android) — feature-detect first; iOS Safari ignores it but doesn't error. Audio feedback short (<100ms) for taps; longer SFX for milestones (level clear, game over). Use Web Audio API with a single shared AudioContext that's RESUMED on first user gesture (iOS suspends audio until user interacts).
guidelines.why: Tactile + audio feedback is what makes mobile games feel responsive. iOS Safari blocks audio until first user gesture — your AudioContext.resume() must happen inside a tap handler, not in your init.
examples: if (navigator.vibrate) navigator.vibrate(20);
let audioContext; function ensureAudio() { if (!audioContext) audioContext = new AudioContext(); if (audioContext.state === 'suspended') audioContext.resume(); }
// Wire ensureAudio() into your first tap handler — don't call from init.

guidelines.rule: Test that the entire game UI fits within a 375×667 viewport (iPhone SE — smallest current iPhone). All controls reachable, no horizontal scroll, no clipped text, no controls under the safe-area inset. If a level/screen needs more vertical room, scroll the playfield; never let critical buttons fall below the fold.
guidelines.why: iPhone SE / mini are still in active use. A game that 'works on iPhone 15 Pro' but is broken on SE has cut out 10% of the audience. Designing for the smallest mobile viewport forces good control density.
examples: Body sizing test: open in DevTools at 375x667, no overflow
Card grid that adapts: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(80px, 1fr));
Score text scales: font-size: clamp(16px, 4vw, 22px);

guidelines.rule: For DRAG-mechanics games (PvZ plant placement, match-three puzzle swipe, Jetpack tap-to-rise): use the Pointer Events API consistently. Capture the pointer with `setPointerCapture` so a finger that drags off the original element keeps firing pointermove on it. Critical for slow drags that exit the source element's bounds.
guidelines.why: Without setPointerCapture, dragging a card off its origin breaks the drag mid-gesture (no more pointermove fires). The user's finger left the original button's bounds, so the browser stops sending events to it.
examples: card.addEventListener('pointerdown', e => { card.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId); dragStart(e); });
card.addEventListener('pointermove', e => { if (dragging) updateDragPosition(e); });
card.addEventListener('pointerup', e => { card.releasePointerCapture(e.pointerId); dropCard(e); });

guidelines.rule: Preserve game state across orientation changes, app-switching, and refreshes. Use localStorage for the current state on every meaningful state change (round start, score change, level clear). On load, check for saved state and offer 'Resume' or 'New Game' prominently — don't auto-resume silently (user might want fresh start).
guidelines.why: Mobile users get interrupted constantly. A game that loses progress on tab-switch feels broken. localStorage save-every-meaningful-event is cheap (microseconds) and recovers from any interruption.
examples: function saveState() { localStorage.setItem(GAME_KEY, JSON.stringify({wave, score, lives, plants})); }
// Call saveState() at: wave-start, score-change, lives-lost, level-clear, game-over
// On load: const saved = localStorage.getItem(GAME_KEY); if (saved) showResumePrompt(JSON.parse(saved));

guidelines.rule: Lane-tap and rhythm games must use FORGIVING hit-detection: when the user taps a lane, hit the LOWEST visible tile in that lane regardless of its exact y position. Do NOT require the tile's bottom edge to have crossed into a narrow strike-zone band before the tap counts. Strict 'must be inside the band' detection feels broken on mobile (humans tap ~80-200ms early in anticipation; sub-pixel timing is impossible with finger input).
guidelines.why: Real incident 2026-04-25: tap-tile rhythm 097 used `if (!target || target.y + target.h < strikeTop) gameOver('You tapped white.')` — meaning a tile that was 99% on-screen but hadn't quite crossed the strike-zone top counted as 'white'. User reported 'I can barely hit a black tile 1 time out of 10.' The strict band-check assumes pixel-perfect human reflexes; real users tap with anticipation. Forgiving lane-mode (tap = hit lowest visible tile in that lane) is the canonical tap-tile rhythm / Beatstar / tap-rhythm game approach.
examples: // CORRECT: forgiving lane-tap
function handleTap(x, y) {
const lane = Math.floor(x / r.width * LANES);
const target = lowestVisibleTileInLane(lane);  // ANY visible tile counts
if (!target) { gameOver('You tapped empty lane.'); return; }
hitTile(target);  // also: score by accuracy = 1 - abs(target.center - strikeCenter) / maxDist
// BAD: strict band-check
// if (target.y + target.h < strikeTop || target.y > strikeBot) gameOver('white');

guidelines.rule: When a game's mechanic isn't immediately obvious from a single screenshot (Stack Tower's slide-and-drop, Pinball's plunger, helix-drop arcade's drag-to-rotate), include a TAP-TO-START overlay with: 1-line goal (`Stack as high as you can`), 1-line how (`Tap to drop the moving block`), 1-line outcome (`Misalign and you lose part of the block`). 3 lines max. The user shouldn't need a tutorial to learn the input.
guidelines.why: Real incident 2026-04-25: Stack Tower 103 had correct mechanics but user reported 'I kind of don't get it but it seems like the play mechanics are a bit odd.' Without an explicit goal/input/outcome explanation, novel mobile mechanics feel broken when they're working as designed. The cost of a 3-line overlay is ~30s of LLM time; the cost of confusion is total — user closes the game.
examples: <div id='startOverlay' class='overlay'>
STACK TOWER
Goal: Stack blocks as high as you can.
How: Tap to drop the moving block when it lines up.
Outcome: Misalign and the overhang is lost — block shrinks each turn.
<button id='startBtn'>PLAY</button>

guidelines.rule: Direction controls (left/right/up/down) MUST use ARROW GLYPHS (◀ ▶ ▲ ▼ or unicode ← → ↑ ↓ or SVG triangles), NEVER text labels like 'Left' / 'Right' / 'Up' / 'Down'. Action buttons (Punch, Fire, Jump, Plant, Spin) MAY use a single short verb but should prefer an icon + verb together (🥊 PUNCH, ▶ PLAY, ⚡ FIRE). Localizing buttons via text breaks for non-English players AND eats horizontal space that's already scarce on mobile.
guidelines.why: Real incident 2026-04-27: Boxing canary 140 shipped with 3 text-labeled buttons 'Move Left | Punch | Move Right' on a portrait phone. The 'Move' prefix is redundant noise; arrows would be instantly recognizable in any language. Text buttons also force wider hit areas which compete for the bottom-strip real estate where actions need to live. Genre convention (every classic mobile fighter, runner, shmup) uses glyphs not labels.
examples: // CORRECT
<button class='dpad-left' aria-label='Move left'>◀</button>
<button class='dpad-right' aria-label='Move right'>▶</button>
<button class='action-punch' aria-label='Punch'>🥊</button>
// BAD
// <button>Move Left</button> <button>Punch</button> <button>Move Right</button>

guidelines.rule: Mobile control LAYOUT must group related controls together using thumb-arc geometry: directional/movement controls form a CLUSTER on one side (D-pad shape OR a single drag-pad zone covering bottom-left ~40% of viewport), action buttons form a CLUSTER on the other side (bottom-right ~30%, stacked or arc-arranged). NEVER scatter movement and action buttons in a single horizontal row across the bottom — players cannot reach the far button with the same thumb that's currently pressing the near one, AND a 'left | action | right' linear strip puts the action button BETWEEN the two direction buttons, blocking thumb travel between them.
guidelines.why: Real incident 2026-04-27: Boxing canary 140 placed Move Left / Punch / Move Right in a single horizontal row at the bottom. Players holding the phone two-handed had to alternate left+right thumbs awkwardly because the action button (Punch) sat in the middle, separating the directional pair. Two-zone touch interaction (left-half = movement, right-half = action) is the canonical mobile fighting/runner layout. PvZ, jetpack side-scroller, endless runner, Mortal Kombat Mobile, every Boxing port — all use cluster-by-thumb geometry.
examples: // CORRECT — cluster geometry
<div class='controls'>
<div class='dpad bottom-left'>  <!-- movement cluster -->
<button class='up'>▲</button>
<button class='left'>◀</button>
<button class='right'>▶</button>
<button class='down'>▼</button>
<div class='actions bottom-right'>  <!-- action cluster -->
<button class='action-jab'>🥊</button>
<button class='action-power'>💥</button>
// BETTER for fighting / racing — TWO-ZONE TOUCH (no buttons at all)
// canvas.addEventListener('pointerdown', e => { if (e.clientX < window.innerWidth/2) startMove(e); else startAction(e); });
// BAD — linear strip splits direction pair with action between
//

guidelines.rule: Set CSS touch-action:none on the game/interactive canvas (and call preventDefault in your touch/pointer handlers where needed) so swiping to play does not scroll, pull-to-refresh, or pinch-zoom the page. Apply it to the playfield, not necessarily the whole document, so any scrollable UI still scrolls.
guidelines.why: By default the browser claims touch gestures for scroll and zoom, so dragging to steer/aim/paint instead scrolls the page or zooms, making the game unplayable. touch-action:none on the canvas hands those gestures to the game. preventDefault on touchmove also stops iOS rubber-band scrolling during play.
examples: CSS: canvas{touch-action:none;display:block}
in a touchmove handler that controls the game: e.preventDefault();
WRONG: dragging on the canvas scrolls the page instead of moving the player

guidelines.rule: Provide on-screen touch controls for anything that uses WASD/arrow keys, the mouse, or a keyboard on desktop. Detect touch (e.g. matchMedia('(pointer: coarse)') or the first touch event) and show a virtual joystick/d-pad for movement, large tap zones or buttons for actions (jump/fire/interact), and on-screen buttons for any keyboard shortcut. Keyboard/mouse still work on desktop.
guidelines.why: A phone has no WASD and no mouse; a desktop-only control scheme is simply unplayable on touch. An on-screen joystick plus action buttons (shown when touch is detected) makes the same game playable everywhere with no separate build. This is the difference between a mobile user enjoying the game and immediately closing it.
examples: show a virtual joystick + Jump/Fire buttons when matchMedia('(pointer: coarse)').matches or on first touchstart
tap zones: left/right halves of the screen to move, tap to act
WRONG: 'Use WASD to move' with no touch alternative

guidelines.rule: NEVER call element.requestPointerLock(), and never gate gameplay or starting the game on it. Pointer Lock is not granted in the in-app WKWebView preview and does not exist on mobile, so a pointer-lock control scheme is completely unplayable there. For look/aim use DRAG-LOOK: accumulate movementX/movementY deltas while dragging (yaw -= dx*sens; pitch -= dy*sens), so turning is unbounded and works with touch.
guidelines.why: requestPointerLock silently fails in the preview and on phones; a 'click to play' that calls it leaves the game stuck on the menu, and an FPS using it can never aim. Delta-accumulating drag-look (mouse-drag on desktop, touch-drag on mobile) works everywhere and is not bounded by the screen edge. Pointer lock is a dead end on these targets.
examples: drag-look: on pointermove while dragging, yaw -= e.movementX*sens; pitch = clamp(pitch - e.movementY*sens, -1.55, 1.55);
start the game unconditionally on tap - do NOT await/gate on requestPointerLock
WRONG: canvas.requestPointerLock() for aim or to begin play

guidelines.rule: Audio must start on the first user tap, never on load. Mobile browsers block autoplay, so unlock the AudioContext (resume it / call the library's start, e.g. Tone.start()) inside the first pointerdown/touch, and show a clear tap-to-start overlay. Keep everything else (visuals/gameplay) running even if audio stays blocked.
guidelines.why: iOS and mobile Safari/WKWebView require a genuine gesture to start audio; calling play/resume at load does nothing and the app is permanently silent. A visible tap-to-start overlay both satisfies the unlock requirement and tells the user what to do. Never block rendering on a suspended audio context - degrade to muted.
examples: overlay.addEventListener('pointerdown', async () => { await unlockAudio(); hideOverlay(); start(); }, { once:true });
if audio cannot start, keep the game fully playable and visually intact, just muted
WRONG: starting music on window load - blocked and silent on mobile

guidelines.rule: Clamp devicePixelRatio to <=2 and keep a lower entity/particle/body budget on mobile. Detect small screens / coarse pointers and reduce particle counts, sprite counts, physics bodies, light counts, and effect intensity, and cap the render resolution at 2x DPR. Keep the experience smooth rather than maxing detail.
guidelines.why: A 3x Retina phone renders 9x the pixels of a 1x display; on a busy scene that is the difference between 60fps and a slideshow. Clamping DPR to 2 and trimming the entity budget on mobile is the highest-ROI performance fix. A smooth, slightly simpler scene beats a gorgeous one stuttering at 10fps.
examples: const dpr = Math.min(window.devicePixelRatio || 1, 2);
const PARTICLES = (innerWidth < 700 || matchMedia('(pointer: coarse)').matches) ? 60 : 160;
lower physics body / sprite caps on mobile

guidelines.rule: The experience MUST be fully usable with TOUCH ALONE - no keyboard, no mouse, no hover required to reach any feature or complete the core loop. Mentally (or actually) walk through it as a phone user: can you start it, control it, trigger every essential action, and reach a win/finish, using only taps and drags? If any step needs a key or hover, add a touch path.
guidelines.why: The acceptance bar for a mobile mini-app is touch-only playability. Many builds render fine on a phone but hide a critical action behind a key press or a hover, so a phone user gets stuck. Explicitly verifying the whole loop with touch catches the gaps that 'it looks fine on mobile' misses.
examples: every documented control has an on-screen touch equivalent
start, play, pause/restart, and any menu are all reachable by tap
WRONG: a game that needs Space to jump or Enter to restart with no on-screen button

guidelines.rule: On phones the screen is small, so NO first-person weapon/viewmodel (3D mesh or sprite) may cover more than ~1/3 of the screen -- keep it bottom-anchored and compact so gameplay stays visible. Any game that uses WASD/arrows/mouse on desktop MUST render on-screen touch controls on mobile (virtual joystick + drag-look + action buttons, each >=44px), and must be fully completable with touch alone.

When you render Unicode game glyphs (chess pieces, the four filled card suits, HUD 'lives' hearts) and color them via CSS, append the U+FE0E text-presentation variation selector to each glyph string — in JS write it as the escape \uFE0E, e.g. '♟\uFE0E', '♠\uFE0E', '♥\uFE0E', '♦\uFE0E', '♣\uFE0E' — and/or set `font-variant-emoji: text` on the container. U+265F (black chess pawn) and the four filled suits ♠♣♥♦ default to COLOR EMOJI on iOS/Safari, which IGNORES your CSS color, text-shadow, and SVG fill, so a white pawn / a red suit / a magenta heart renders as a wrong-colored emoji. U+265F is the ONLY chess codepoint with default emoji presentation (♔ through ♞ are text-default and already honor CSS color), which is why only PAWNS invert. CAVEAT: U+FE0E only works on codepoints that HAVE a defined text-variation sequence — it is a NO-OP for emoji-default glyphs without one, e.g. ⚪/⚫ (U+26AA/26AB medium circles, often used as checkers/draughts pieces) and the 🎲 game-die emoji; for those use a CSS/SVG shape or a text-default codepoint instead.
guidelines.why: On iOS/Safari, emoji-presentation codepoints render as full-color emoji and ignore CSS color/text-shadow/SVG fill. A chess mini-app colored its solid pawn glyph white via .piece.white, but iOS showed a dark emoji pawn (verified 2026-07-01) while every other piece rendered correctly — only U+265F is emoji-default. Card games hit the identical bug via ♠♣♥♦. Desktop renders all of these as text, so the bug is INVISIBLE on the macOS preview and only shows up on a phone.
examples: WRONG: const GLYPH = { pawn: '♟' }; .piece.white{color:#fff} — iOS shows a color pawn emoji ignoring the white
WRONG: `♥` — iOS renders a color heart emoji, not a red text heart
GOOD: const GLYPH = { pawn: '♟\uFE0E' }; (or set font-variant-emoji:text on the piece/card/suit elements)
GOOD: livesEl.textContent = '♥\uFE0E'.repeat(lives) so the HUD heart honors your CSS color
N/A: checkers built from '⚫'/'⚪' cannot be fixed with U+FE0E (no text variation sequence) — use a CSS/SVG circle

guidelines.rule: Any game/app with a GRID or BOARD or a row/hand of repeated pieces (cards, chess/checkers pieces, tiles, dominoes, mahjong, gems, a 2048/match-3 grid, a poker board) MUST lay out responsively so nothing overlaps, clips off-screen, or overflows horizontally on a phone. Rules that always apply: (1) size the board/pieces in relative units or clamp to the viewport — e.g. `width:min(92vw, 560px)` for the board, and derive piece/cell size from it — so it fits the narrowest phone; NEVER a fixed desktop pixel canvas that gets squeezed. (2) A row of items (community cards, a captured-pieces tray, a tile rack) either fits the width or wraps/scrolls WITHIN its own container — it must not spill onto neighbors. (3) When enlarging elements on request ('make the pieces bigger'), scale proportionally at EACH @media breakpoint and re-verify the fit; do NOT hardcode one big base size. (4) Give the board/main-play-area the most space; fold controls/settings into a compact bar or collapsible panel. This is genre-agnostic — card games, board games, and tile/puzzle games all break the same way when a desktop-sized layout is shrunk to a phone.
guidelines.why: The mChatAI Playability Gate now runs a mobile-viewport LAYOUT check (PG.B3, 2026-07-02) on every branch across genres — horizontal overflow + off-screen clipping (deterministic) and overlap/unreadable (vision). A layout that overflows or overlaps on a phone will be FLAGGED (and reads as broken to users) even if the game logic works. Verified on a Texas Hold'em where oversized cards overlapped the board/pot on mobile while looking fine on desktop; the same failure mode applies to any grid/board/hand game.
examples: GOOD: `.board{width:min(92vw,560px);aspect-ratio:1}` then cells = board/8 — fits every phone
GOOD: `.hand{display:flex;gap:6px;overflow-x:auto}` so a long rack scrolls inside itself, not over the board
WRONG: a 1300px absolute-positioned 'table' with seats at fixed px, shrunk to a 390px phone → pieces collide
WRONG (iteration): bumping a base `.card`/`.piece` width to a big value without matching the @media rules → overflow on mobile

guidelines.rule: Wrap ALL on-screen touch controls (d-pads, joysticks, action buttons) in ONE container carrying data-mchatai="touch-controls" -- prefer mounting the ui.touch-controls Lego component, which does this for you. The container must (a) show only on touch/coarse-pointer devices and stay hidden on desktop, (b) hide while the native mChatAI controller overlay is active (listen for window CustomEvent 'mchatai:virtualgamepad' with detail {active:true|false}), and (c) never be the ONLY input path: every control must map to a keyboard handler the game also supports. Cover EVERY input axis the game logic reads -- if the code moves forward/back/left/right, the surface needs all four, not just steering.
guidelines.why: On-screen controls baked into the page are clutter on desktop (a keyboard exists) and DOUBLE controls on iOS when the user brings up the platform's built-in D-Pad overlay, which synthesizes real keyboard events. The single marked container is the platform contract that lets every layer (desktop, iOS overlay, install-time backstop) hide or show the surface deterministically. An incomplete surface (steering but no forward button) makes the game boring or unplayable on the very devices the controls exist for.
examples: import { TouchControls } from './web-components/ui/TouchControls.js'; TouchControls.mount(document.body, { dpad:['up','down','left','right'], actions:[{label:'JUMP', key:' '}] })

hand-rolled:
...buttons...
plus a window listener for mchatai:virtualgamepad that toggles it
WRONG: control buttons scattered in the DOM with no shared marked container (nothing can hide them under the native D-Pad)
WRONG: a runner game whose touch surface has left/right only -- the accelerate control the game loop reads is missing
